newsitem.title: KAZAKHSTAN: Two cosmonauts back on Earth after 6 months on Mir.
newsitem.headline: Two cosmonauts back on Earth after 6 months on Mir.

text.p: Two Russian cosmonauts who spent six months on the Mir space station landed safely in the steppes of Kazakhstan on Thursday after one of the toughest missions in the history of manned space flight.

The blackened Soyuz capsule, dangling beneath a huge white and yellow brake parachute, floated smoothly down to the barren Kazakh steppeland shortly before 4:20 p.m. Moscow time (1220 GMT), slightly behind schedule.
Commander Vasily Tsibliyev and flight engineer Alexander Lazutkin, looking tired but well, smiled broadly as they were escorted from the capsule into the blazing Kazakh sunlight.
Tsibliyev, who seemed to be the more animated of the two, said he felt "happy to be back on Earth".
The cosmonauts have endured a series of major setbacks since they arrived on board Mir in February. The most serious was a June 25 collision between the station and its supply ship.
Mir has run on partial power since then. They also had to contend with a fire and a series of problems with their life support systems during their mission.

Helicopters bearing rescue teams clattered to the remote site as soon as Soyuz landed. The two men gulped down water and doctors carried out medical checks on them in an orange tent inflated near the site of the landing.
There had been some concern about the health of Tsibliyev, 43, who developed a stress-related cardiac problem while on Mir.
"Tsibliyev is in good condition. There is nothing out of the ordinary," said Igor Goncharov, the mission's head doctor.

The cosmonauts were flown by helicopter to Dzhezkazgan where they underwent further tests, signed autographs for excited officials from Mission Control and, with support, went to greet local people who gave them gifts of Kazakh hats and costumes.
"The cosmonauts are back...We are fully satisfied with their condition," Yuri Glaskov, deputy director of the Star City cosmonauts' training centre, told reporters in Dzhezkazgan.
Asked about the many problems that have occurred on Mir during the two Russians' six-month stay, Glaskov said: "We will talk to them about this later and will sort it all out."
But at Mission Control near Moscow deputy fight director Viktor Blagov suggested that Tsibliyev would have some hard questions to answer in due course about the June 25 collision.

"We have found not a single fault in the systems of either Mir or Progress (the supply ship) during the collision. A logical conclusion follows -- technology was not at fault," Blagov told a news conference.
President Boris Yeltsin said last week human error may have been to blame for the crash, which threatened Mir's future.
But on Thursday Yeltsin sent a message of thanks to the two cosmonauts, praising the "persistence, courage and heroism they showed during their mission".
In a statement, Yeltsin wished them a speedy recovery from their gruelling ordeal and their continued active participation in Russia's space programme.
Live television pictures at Mission Control had shown Soyuz with Tsibliyev, and Lazutkin, 39, on board departing from Mir at 12:56 p.m. Moscow time (0856 GMT).
There appeared to be a three-minute delay in the operation compared to the original schedule but a Mission Control operator said the undocking went well.
"Everything is all right with you," the operator told the crew. "Thank God," replied Tsibliyev.
Tsibliyev and Lazutkin have left British-born Michael Foale and their two Russian replacements, Commander Anatoly Solovyov and engineer Pavel Vinogradov, aboard Mir.
"I hope that everything bad that we've had will leave with us," Tsibliyev said in a live broadcast from Mir.
"We are leaving. See you on Earth."
A Mission Control operator told Tsibliyev and Lazutkin: "Thank you for the job you've done. Happy landing."
The cosmonauts wore lightweight spacesuits during their return, each weighing 10 kg with independent air supply systems.
The light spacesuits were introduced in 1973 after three cosmonauts -- Georgy Dobrovolsky, Vladislav Volkov and Viktor Patsayev -- died during descent in 1971 in a capsule which lost air.
Tsibliyev and Lazutkin travelled later on Thursday by plane to Chkalovsky military airbase near Moscow. A bus was due to take them on to Star City where they were to be reunited with their families.
"They may go home after seven or 10 days, but they will be able to see their families during this period," said Pyotr Klimuk, head of the Cosmonauts' Training Centre.
